newsitem.title: YEMEN: Yemen kidnappers seize seven German tourists.
newsitem.headline: Yemen kidnappers seize seven German tourists.

text.p: Yemeni kidnappers have seized seven German tourists travelling in southeastern Yemen on motorcycles, a local police official said on Wednesday.

Hadramaut police chief Ali Nasser Lakhshaa told Reuters the men were seized by gunmen in the Wadi al-Dabaat between Mahra and Hadramaut provinces two days ago. He said their local travel agency reported their abduction on Tuesday.

Official sources said the kidnappers, all local tribesmen, wanted to put pressure on the government to bring to justice an alleged Yemeni swindler who sold them smuggled cars brought in from Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states.

"The man was held by local authorities for 17 days before disappearing," the source told Reuters. "They are trying to put pressure on the government to bring him to justice and to have their money returned."

A Yemeni security source in Sanaa had earlier put the number of abducted German tourists at five and said their abductors had telephoned local authorities to ask for 12 million marks ($7 million) ransom to free them.
Lakhshaa said security forces in Hadramaut -- 650 km (406 miles) east of the southern port city of Aden -- were put on alert and were doing all they could to find the Germans and their kidnappers.
He denied the kidnappers were demanding a ransom.
The Yemeni tour operator was not immediately available for comment and Yemeni officials gave no further details.
Yemeni tribes with grievances against the government or foreign oil companies have kidnapped scores of tourists, diplomats or other foreigners in recent years to use as bargaining chips.
An American diplomat and a Saudi ambassador have been among the kidnap victims. There have been no reported casualties from the abductions and all of the hostages have been released unharmed.
Some were rescued by security forces, others were set free.
An American oil engineer kidnapped by a Yemeni mountain tribe was released on February 26 after being held for 16 days.

His kidnappers had demanded a compensation of $2 million or the return of a piece of land in Sanaa which they said was given to one of their tribal leaders. It was not clear whether their demands were met in return for the engineer's release.
